Cycle-1 full pre-registration sweep: Not ready - 2 blocking issues, 2 non-blocking hygiene issues, 1 suggestion.

Verdict: Not ready for registration. The curator-bounded universe can use `claim_type=candidate_rebuild`, but the current source plan and Year values do not support registration: the artifacts claim 16 per-philosopher Wikipedia pages supply every Primary Work/Year/Tradition cell, while several exact Year cells rely on uncited per-work pages or are contradicted/unsupported by the cited source set.

Findings:
1. Current `source_urls`/`source_count` under-ground the Year column.
   - Type/severity: structural, BLOCKING.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `draft.json::source_count = 16` and `source_urls` contains only one per-philosopher Wikipedia article per staged philosopher. `curation.json::source_coverage_notes` says each per-philosopher article supplies Primary Work, Year, and Tradition. But `draft.json::_extraction_notes` admits the Year cell is taken from "the per-work Wikipedia article or the philosopher's article", and several spot-checks confirm the exact work-year value is not fully available from the cited per-philosopher page alone.
   - Evidence from staged ground-truth source set: Plato's cited article lists `Republic` only in a multi-item `Notable works` list and does not provide the c. 375 BC publication date there (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato`, Notable works lines 377-390). Aristotle's cited article lists `Nicomachean Ethics` among several notable works but gives no c. 340 BC date (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle`, lines 427-433). Marcus Aurelius's cited article says he wrote `Meditations` while on campaign between 170 and 180, not in exactly 175 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius`, lines 750-758). Work pages not in the staged source set supply some of the missing dates: `Republic (Plato)` says published c. 375 BC (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_(Plato)`, lines 226-240), and `Summa Theologica` says composed 1265-1274 / unfinished at Aquinas's death in 1274 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica`, lines 177-193).
   - Impact: the row values may be repairable, but the registered source set currently does not ground all cells it claims to ground. Because source_count/source_urls are part of registration metadata, this is blocking.
   - Minimal repair: either add the necessary per-work Wikipedia URLs to `source_urls` and update `source_count`, source roles, `temporal_note`, and `_extraction_notes`; or restrict/normalize Year cells to values demonstrably supplied by the 16 existing per-philosopher articles.

2. Aristotle `Year = -340` is not supported by the source evidence and appears factually wrong under the cited Wikipedia normalization rule.
   - Type/severity: factual, BLOCKING.
   - Evidence from staged CSV: `Aristotle,Nicomachean Ethics,-340,Classical Greek`.
   - Evidence from staged ground-truth source set: Aristotle's article identifies `Nicomachean Ethics` as a notable work but gives no `c. 340 BC` date for it (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle`, lines 427-433). The same article's ethics navigation list later labels `Nicomachean Ethics` as `c. 322 BC`, not c. 340 BC (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle`, lines 2471-2475).
   - Evidence from validation/challenge source: the `Nicomachean Ethics` article says no consensus dates the composition; it gives 353 BCE as a terminus post quem for part of the work and says the traditional position places it in Aristotle's last Athens period, 335 BCE to 322 BCE (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachean_Ethics`, lines 211-214). This contradicts the staged `-340` scalar.
   - Impact: even if a scalar is needed, `-340` is not defensible from the current source set. This is a cell-level factual blocker.
   - Minimal repair: replace with a source-grounded scalar such as `-322` if using the source's c. 322 BC label, or revise the schema/year convention to allow a range/approximation for ancient works; document the scalarization rule.

3. `candidate_rebuild` is the right claim type, but the prompt/universe wording should expose the candidate nature more clearly.
   - Type/severity: scope-related, SUGGESTION.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `curation.json::claim_type = candidate_rebuild`, and the decision log correctly explains that no clean Wikipedia master list defines "major Western philosophers". Under the curation workflow, `candidate_rebuild` is appropriate when the universe is curator-bounded rather than sourced from a master list; `partially_supplemented` would imply a source-defined base universe with supplement rows, which this instance does not have.
   - Evidence from validation/challenge source: Wikipedia's `Timeline of Western philosophers` is a direct Wiki-family list of Western-tradition philosophers but is far too broad for the staged 16-row canon and includes many omitted figures such as Spinoza, Russell, Frege, Husserl, Epicurus, Zeno, and others (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Western_philosophers`, search/discovery result). That supports the curator's claim that a broad list exists but not a clean "major 16" list.
   - Impact: not blocking under `candidate_rebuild`, but the benchmark-facing title `List the major Western philosophers...` reads more exhaustive than the metadata claim. A cleaner prompt would say `List a curated set of 16 major Western philosophers...` or otherwise expose that the row universe is a candidate canon.

4. `Primary Work` cells are mostly plausible, but source_coverage overstates article support for a single "most-canonical" designation.
   - Type/severity: structural, NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `normalization_decisions` honestly describes curator judgment for Plato, Aristotle, Hume, and Marx, but `source_coverage_notes` says each article supplies the Primary Work designation. The per-philosopher pages often supply a notable-work list rather than a single primary-work ranking.
   - Evidence from staged source set and validation: Hume's article strongly supports `A Treatise of Human Nature` as the row's primary work and dates it 1739-1740 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume`, lines 307-345 and 1083-1086). Marx's article calls `Das Kapital` his major life's work and says Volume I was published in 1867 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx`, lines 566-571). Kant's article supports `Critique of Pure Reason` as the critical text emerging in 1781 and calls it highly significant (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immanuel_Kant`, lines 491-505 and 548-549). By contrast, Aristotle's article lists several notable works together, while the `Nicomachean Ethics` work article says only that it is Aristotle's best-known work on ethics, not clearly his overall single most-canonical work (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle`, lines 427-433; `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachean_Ethics`, lines 187-190).
   - Impact: not blocking if the qualitative column is allowed to be curator-selected, but the provenance wording should be softened to `curator-selected among source-listed notable works`, rather than `supplies the Primary Work designation`.

5. Source URL order documentation is stale.
   - Type/severity: structural, NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `source_coverage_notes` says `source_urls[0..15]` are alphabetical by Philosopher, but `draft.json::source_urls` begins Plato, Aristotle, Marcus Aurelius, Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, then proceeds chronologically/era-wise. The CSV itself is alphabetically sorted by Philosopher.
   - Impact: no row-value impact; it can confuse index-based source-role review.
   - Minimal repair: either reorder source_urls alphabetically to match the note/CSV, or change the note to say the URLs are era ordered.

Pass checks and spot checks:
- Claim type: PASS. `candidate_rebuild` is more defensible than `partially_supplemented` because there is no master source universe to supplement; per-row value sourcing does not change the universe-level claim.
- Source_count set membership: PASS. There are 16 source URLs and 16 staged rows, and each URL corresponds to one staged philosopher. The mismatch is grounding depth/order, not count.
- Row-level spot checks that pass under current/expanded evidence: Descartes `Meditations on First Philosophy` 1641 is supported by the Descartes article (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/René_Descartes`, lines 647 and 953); Hume `A Treatise of Human Nature` 1739 is supported as first major work / 1739-1740 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume`, lines 307-345 and 1083-1086); Kant `Critique of Pure Reason` 1781 is supported (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immanuel_Kant`, lines 491-505); Marx `Das Kapital` 1867 is supported (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx`, lines 566-571); Nietzsche `Thus Spoke Zarathustra` 1885 is supported as an 1883-1885 work if the scalarization rule is completed-work year (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche`, lines 751-760); Wittgenstein `Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus` 1921 is supported (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Wittgenstein`, lines 426 and 985-987); Sartre `Being and Nothingness` 1943 is supported (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre`, lines 388 and 887-894).
- Tradition classifications: PASS at audit depth. The six traditions are conventional enough for this qualitative/candidate instance: Marcus Aurelius is reasonably Hellenistic-Roman given his Roman/Stoic context; Augustine and Aquinas are reasonably Medieval; Wittgenstein, Heidegger, and Sartre are reasonably 20th-c. Contemporary under the stated cutoff.
- Preflight: PASS except for the source-grounding blockers above. CSV has 16 rows x 4 columns; `Philosopher` primary key is unique; no blank cells; CSV header equals `draft.json::columns`; `source_count = 16 = len(source_urls)`; `claim_type = candidate_rebuild`; `query_category = qualitative`, `secondary_category = temporal`, and `operation_type = projection`; `domain = Culture/Philosophy` follows the taxonomy's `Family/Subdomain` preference.

Final counts:
- Severity: BLOCKING 2 / NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE 2 / SUGGESTION 1.
- Issue type counts: factual 1 / structural 3 / scope-related 1.
- Ready / Not ready: Not ready.

Minimal fixes needed before registration:
1. Add the per-work Wikipedia URLs needed to support exact Year cells, or revise the source plan to values supported by the existing 16 per-philosopher URLs.
2. Repair Aristotle's Year cell and document the ancient-work scalarization rule.
3. Optional cleanup: soften Primary Work provenance wording, fix the source URL order note, and consider making the title expose the `curated set of 16` nature of the candidate universe.

Cycle-2 full pre-registration sweep: Ready - 0 blocking issues, 2 non-blocking hygiene issues, 1 suggestion.

Verdict: Ready for registration. The cycle-1 blocking issues are resolved at the row/source level: the CSV now has Aristotle `Year = -322` and Marcus Aurelius `Year = 180`, and `draft.json::source_count = 32 = len(source_urls)` with 16 per-philosopher URLs plus 16 per-work URLs. The remaining issues are narrative/provenance cleanup only; they do not change the row set, PK, source_count field, or row-level Year support.

Findings:
1. Several narrative fields still preserve cycle-0 source-count and Year wording as if current.
   - Type/severity: structural, NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `draft.json::source_count` is now 32 and `source_urls[16..31]` contain the per-work URLs, but `draft.json::_extraction_notes` still says `source_count = 16`, says only one per-philosopher Wikipedia article per row was fetched, and still gives old example values `Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics c. 340 BC = -340` and `Marcus Aurelius's Meditations c. 175 AD = 175 positive`. `curation.json::collection_summary` also still says per-row cells are source-grounded from each philosopher's individual Wikipedia article with `source_count = 16`. The pre-gate/source-plan bullets in `decision_log` still state `source_count = 16`, while the later post-audit paragraph correctly says `source_count 16 -> 32`. `normalization_decisions` still contains the old Year-normalization examples `Aristotle ... c. 340 BC = -340`, `Marcus Aurelius Meditations c. 175 AD`, and the old era-boundary phrase `Marcus Aurelius 175 AD`.
   - Evidence from staged ground-truth source set: the repaired values are source-grounded: `Nicomachean Ethics` gives the traditional composition window as 335 BCE to Aristotle's death in 322 BCE (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachean_Ethics`, Background lines 211-214), and `Meditations` says Marcus Aurelius was emperor from 161-180 CE and that large portions may have been written during AD 170-180 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations`, lead/composition lines 163-168).
   - Impact: this is not blocking because the CSV and machine-readable source_count/source_urls fields are correct and the post-audit paragraph records the repair. It is still confusing registration prose.
   - Minimal repair: update `collection_summary`, `_extraction_notes`, the initial source-plan/pre-gate bullets in `decision_log`, and `normalization_decisions` to the current 32-URL pattern and current Aristotle/Marcus Year values. If old values are retained for history, mark them explicitly as superseded cycle-0 values.

2. Primary Work provenance still overstates what the per-philosopher pages prove.
   - Type/severity: structural, NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `draft.json::temporal_note` says the `Primary Work` designation reflects each philosopher's most-cited and most-anthologized text per the per-philosopher Wikipedia article, and `curation.json::source_coverage_notes` says the per-philosopher articles supply the Primary Work designation from lead / Notable works / Major works. This is too strong for pages that list multiple works without ranking one as the single primary work.
   - Evidence from staged ground-truth source set: Aristotle's page lists `Organon`, `Physics`, `Metaphysics`, `Nicomachean Ethics`, `Politics`, `Rhetoric`, and `Poetics` together under Notable works, and later calls several treatises important (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle`, infobox/lead lines 427-494). The `Nicomachean Ethics` page supports the row's work choice within ethics, but it does not independently prove that it is Aristotle's single overall most-canonical work (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachean_Ethics`, lead/background lines 187-213). Hume is better supported because the Treatise article calls `A Treatise of Human Nature` Hume's most important work and one of the most influential works in philosophy (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Human_Nature`, lead lines 158-176), but the mixed pattern shows the provenance language should be softer.
   - Impact: not blocking under `claim_type=candidate_rebuild` because the qualitative `Primary Work` column is explicitly curator-selected. The source set supports the works as major/notable, but not always the exact single-work ranking.
   - Minimal repair: change wording to `curator-selected canonical primary work, chosen from source-listed major/notable works and documented in normalization_decisions`; avoid saying every per-philosopher article itself supplies a single most-cited/most-anthologized designation.

3. `candidate_rebuild` remains the correct claim type, but the table title still reads more exhaustive than the candidate universe.
   - Type/severity: scope-related, SUGGESTION.
   - Evidence from staged artifacts: `curation.json::claim_type = candidate_rebuild` and the curation notes correctly state that no single Wikipedia master list defines `the major Western philosophers` as a clean 16-row universe. Adding per-work URLs does not make the universe source-defined; it only fixes cell-level grounding. Under the curation workflow, `partially_supplemented` is for a source-defined base universe with added supplement rows, and `source_defined` requires a source-defined row universe. This instance still has a curator-bounded universe, so `candidate_rebuild` is the right claim type.
   - Evidence from validation/challenge sources: Wikipedia's `Western philosophy` article names omitted early-modern and 20th-century figures such as Spinoza, Leibniz, Russell, Husserl, and Frege as important/influential in the history of Western philosophy (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_philosophy`, early modern lines 427-431 and contemporary/analytic lines 492-512). Wikipedia's `Timeline of Western philosophers` is explicitly a broad list of Western-tradition philosophers and includes many more figures than the staged 16 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Western_philosophers`, introduction and list lines 124-174; 20th-century list lines 467-550).
   - Impact: not blocking because the curation record honestly declares candidate_rebuild and open_questions discuss expansion/narrowing. For benchmark-facing clarity, the title could say `a curated set of 16 major Western philosophers...` rather than `the major Western philosophers...`.

Pass checks and spot checks:
- Year-cell source-grounding: PASS. The new 32-URL pattern resolves the cycle-1 source-under-grounding blocker. Spot checks: Plato `Republic` -375 is supported by the `Republic` article's c. 375 BC publication line (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_(Plato)`, lines 226-239); Aristotle `Nicomachean Ethics` -322 is supported by the 335-322 BCE composition-window/latest-year convention (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomachean_Ethics`, lines 211-214); Marcus Aurelius `Meditations` 180 is supported by the 170-180 composition context/latest-year convention (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations`, lines 163-168); Augustine `The City of God` 426 is supported by the completed-work publication line (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_of_God`, lines 160-162); Aquinas `Summa Theologica` 1274 is supported by the 1265-1274 composed range and unfinished-at-death-in-1274 line (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica`, lines 177-193); Hume `A Treatise of Human Nature` 1739 is supportable under the first-publication-year convention from the 1739-40 publication line (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Human_Nature`, lines 158-171); Nietzsche `Thus Spoke Zarathustra` 1885 is supportable under the completed-work convention because the article says the four volumes were published between 1883 and 1885 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thus_Spoke_Zarathustra`, lines 208-215).
- Convention consistency: PASS with the wording caveat in Finding 1. Ancient/medieval composition windows use latest/completed-by year (`-322`, `180`, `426`, `1274`); modern works use first-edition publication year. Hume is not a blocker despite the 1739-40 source range because the curation convention treats modern first-publication year as the scalar, and the source includes 1739.
- Additional per-work checks: Machiavelli `The Prince` 1532 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prince`, lines 228-235), Descartes `Meditations on First Philosophy` 1641 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_on_First_Philosophy`, lines 146-160), Locke `An Essay Concerning Human Understanding` 1689 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Essay_Concerning_Human_Understanding`, lines 131-145), Kant `Critique of Pure Reason` 1781 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critique_of_Pure_Reason`, lines 192-203), Hegel `Phenomenology of Spirit` 1807 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenomenology_of_Spirit`, lines 149-159), Marx `Das Kapital` 1867 for Volume I / first publication (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital`, lines 211-232), Wittgenstein `Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus` 1921 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tractatus_Logico-Philosophicus`, lines 151-174), Heidegger `Being and Time` 1927 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Being_and_Time`, lines 152-177), and Sartre `Being and Nothingness` 1943 (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Being_and_Nothingness`, lines 147-171) all match the staged Year cells.
- Claim type: PASS. `candidate_rebuild` is more defensible than `partially_supplemented` or `source_defined` because the row universe is not derived from a source-defined master list; per-work URLs source cell values only.
